title: The garden
hook: gardens under which rivers flow, and peace as the greeting there (10:10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, raji'un, and your line: a return. Did you share one good memory of someone who has died? Today, where the Qur'an says the return leads. The last of the book's great themes. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Gardens beneath which rivers flow. This path met that phrase on the day about water, and the Qur'an comes back to it again and again when it speaks of what follows death. Shade that doesn't move. Water that doesn't run out. Fruit within reach. It's a picture anyone can see with their eyes shut. And yet the book says the real thing is hidden. What it does tell, very plainly, is what people there say to each other. One word, and it's an ordinary one.

The word is jannah, a garden. It comes from the root j-n-n, to cover or hide. A garden is a place covered by trees, shaded from view. The same root gives jinn, beings hidden from sight; janin, a child hidden in the womb; and junnah, a shield. So paradise, in Arabic, sounds like a covered, sheltered place. The root fits a promise the book keeps. Surah thirty-two says no soul knows what delight is kept hidden for them. And a hadith qudsi in al-Bukhari has Allah say: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined. The rivers and the shade are pictures; the reality, the hadith says, is beyond them. Then surah Yunus, verse ten, gives the sound of the place. In Pickthall's translation: "and their greeting therein will be: Peace." Salam. In surah fifty-six, the people of the garden hear no idle talk and no sin, only the words peace, peace. And in surah thirty-six, peace is a word sent to them from a merciful Lord. Here's the quiet surprise. Muslims say as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, when they meet, and at the end of every prayer. The greeting the book gives to the garden is already in daily use. In this vocabulary, a salam on a street corner is an echo of the garden.

The practice: picture peace. Close your eyes. Let a garden come: shade, the sound of water moving somewhere close, nothing you have to do. Don't build it too carefully; the hadith says the real one is beyond imagining anyway. Just let your shoulders drop into it. Now imagine someone you love walking toward you there, and the only word either of you needs is peace. Salam. Let that word sit in your chest for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Jannah. The garden, from j-n-n, covered and sheltered: rivers beneath, delights still hidden, and peace as the greeting there. Today's word.

Your line: their greeting is peace. These weeks ran from they are one family, through mercy first and held in trust, to a return. Today, greet three people with peace, and mean it. Next, the prophets' own prayers. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims greet each other with as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, the greeting the Qur'an gives to the people of the garden, and end each prayer with it.

a hadith qudsi says it holds what no eye has seen and no heart imagined.

the greeting of the garden is the Muslims' everyday greeting

fork.setup: the people of the garden meet one another. what is their greeting, according to 10:10?
fork.reveal: peace: salam. the same word Muslims use every time they meet.

original.note: Arabic: a garden; paradise. from j-n-n, to cover.

trapdoor: what you thought: paradise is a vague reward somewhere in the sky.
what it means: jannah is a sheltered garden with rivers beneath, where the greeting is peace.
what a scholar hears: j-n-n links jannah to jinn, janin and junnah (shield): the covered, the hidden; 32:17 keeps its delights hidden.

notes: Pickthall wording of the phrase from 10:10 quoted from memory; please confirm.
'More than thirty times' for 'gardens beneath which rivers flow': the phrase occurs over thirty times by common counts; confirm.
Hadith number (Bukhari 3244) cited from memory; confirm.
The j-n-n family (jannah, jinn, janin, junnah) follows standard lexicons; confirm.
Carry is the close of 'the book's great themes' (664–687) and points to the prophets' du'as (688–695).

Editor review 2026-10-01: hook rewritten. It opened 'Picture the first listeners again' (banned opener; the desert-listeners angle was also used on 669 and 670), claimed 'more than thirty times' and 'the most beautiful sentence imaginable' (unsourced count and superlative), and told the listener 'when you get there... the first word you'll hear' (narrator promising paradise, and 'first word' is not in 10:10). It now opens on the phrase itself and calls back day 670. Teach: 'given so people can hope' and 'every time they meet' trimmed; 'every hello is a rehearsal for the garden' softened to an echo, framed as the tradition's vocabulary.
